To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) lead deposition in venison carcasses was greatest with rapid expanding bullets, 2) lead was deposited in muscle tissues with shotgun pellets and black powder bullets, 3) lead deposits were greatest in the abdominal cavity, 4) rinsing the abdominal area spread lead deposits throughout the carcass, 5) lead deposition was greatest in the first 3 days after harvest, 6) lead deposition decreased over time, and

1) lead is present in venison from animals shot with centerfire rifle bullets; 2) rinsing the abdominal area of a deer carcass may spread lead contamination to other parts of the carcass; 3) copper bullets do not deposit lead in muscle tissue; 4) lead deposition is less in animals shot with shotgun or muzzleloader ammunition; and 5) some centerfire bullets are designed to resist fragmentation, and these bullets may be an acceptable alternative to lead bullets for hunters
lead deposition in muscle tissue was greatest with the 3 types of bullets that were designed to fragment upon impacting the animal.
